name: Grounding / earthing mat

card.summary: Conductive sheets and mats meant to connect the sleeper to the earth, with no strong published evidence for sleep or appearance benefits.
card.note: No trials exist; it is classed as an alternative medicine practice.

quick.overview:
Grounding or earthing products are conductive mats, sheets or bands that plug into a wall socket's ground port or a ground rod. Marketing and community posts say sleeping connected to the earth improves sleep and reduces inflammation.
Encyclopedic sources list earthing as an alternative medicine practice. No trials were retrieved for this entry.
quick.mechanism: Proponents claim that electrons from the earth's surface neutralise free radicals in the body. No published mechanistic evidence supports this.
quick.risks: The product is a passive conductive fabric, but connection through a wall outlet raises electrical-safety questions that manufacturers address with built-in resistors; no safety data are published.

lead: Grounding, also called earthing, is the practice of making direct contact with the earth, or with conductive products wired to it, on the belief that this benefits health. Grounding mats, sheets and patches are conductive fabrics that connect to the ground port of a wall socket or to a ground rod, so the user can stay connected while sleeping or sitting at a desk. [1]

People who use them are mostly after better sleep, lower stress and less soreness, and in appearance-focused circles the pitch is the downstream payoff: sounder sleep and recovery are said to show up as a more rested face, calmer skin and more energy for training. Proponents also describe lower inflammation, which they link to skin and recovery.[2][3]

Research on grounding is small. A 2019 randomized trial in 16 massage therapists at a wellness centre examined grounding, pain and quality of life, and reviews written by grounding advocates summarise earlier work on inflammation, sleep and pain. [2][3][4] Wikipedia describes earthing in its energy medicine article, where it notes that skeptics criticise it, and Healthline describes the field as under-researched, with few independent high-quality studies. [8][7] No study cited here has tested grounding mats against facial appearance.

chain: Conductive mat or sheet connects the sleeper to the earth

angle.text: Users sleep on or work with a grounded mat in the belief that it improves sleep quality and reduces inflammation. Appearance-minded users connect that to a fresher look and better recovery between workouts.

infobox: Wall-outlet ground port or ground rod [1]

paras: Products are conductive mats, sheets, bands and patches meant to connect the user to the earth's potential, usually via a wall outlet ground. [1] Barefoot contact with soil, grass or sand is the original form of the practice and is the form most trials describe. [4]
Healthline distinguishes the practice from the psychological grounding techniques used for anxiety, which involve sensory focus exercises rather than electrical contact. [7]

Proponents propose that contact with the earth lets electrons from the ground neutralise free radicals in the body, reducing inflammation, and a 2023 article in the Biomedical Journal calls grounding a possible anti-inflammatory approach. [2] Wikipedia's account says earthing practitioners describe the body as gaining electrons from the surface of the earth, giving the body's circuits a stabilised electric reference point, and that they claim effects on chronic inflammation, ageing-related disorders, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, arthritis, autoimmune disorders, depression and other conditions. [8] Healthline calls this the earthing hypothesis. [7]
A 2020 review in Explore argues that earthing should be part of integrative and lifestyle medicine and collects research evidence and clinical observations in support. [3]

Wikipedia says the practice is promoted by the Earthing Institute, which recommends going barefoot and even removing floors and carpets, and cites a 2011 literature review by Chevalier and colleagues, noting that several of its authors had financial ties to a company promoting earthing. Skeptics and medical commentators such as Steven Novella have criticised the research as pseudoscience, with Novella describing company-linked studies as designed to generate false positives. [8]

A randomized controlled trial published in 2019 in Explore enrolled sixteen massage therapists (mean age 42.8) at the Chopra Center in California to test the effects of grounding on pain and quality of life. [4] Healthline summarises a number of small studies: 16 massage therapists over four weeks showing a trend toward stress reduction, 16 massage therapists over one week reporting less pain, stress, depression and fatigue, 21 people with diabetes who grounded one hour daily for a month and showed faster wound healing, and 20 preterm infants in Indonesia grounded one hour daily for 30 days who had shorter respiratory infections. [7]

The same article lists caveats: small samples, self-reported outcomes, no accounting for placebo effects, uncontrolled variables and possible conflicts of interest. [7] No studies found that test grounding mats for skin or facial appearance.

Healthline considers natural grounding such as walking on grass or sand relatively safe and says mats and devices may carry a risk of electrical shock, advising users to follow instructions closely and to check with a health professional first if they have a chronic condition, an implant or recent surgery. [7]

Grounding is mentioned only occasionally on looksmax.org. One thread praises walking barefoot on grass and stone, saying shoes and socks feel constricting, and a reply jokes that you are taller barefoot. [5] Posts about grounding techniques for anxiety, a different use of the word, also circulate there. [6]

timeline.event: Chevalier and colleagues publish a literature review on earthing; Wikipedia notes author ties to an earthing company. [8]
Randomized trial of grounding in 16 massage therapists published in Explore. [4]
Biomedical Journal review calls grounding an anti-inflammatory approach. [2]

lore.intro: Grounding in looksmaxxing spaces is mostly barefoot-outdoors enthusiasm and passing mentions; mats are marketed with sleep and inflammation claims.[5][2]

claims.claim: Sleeping grounded improves sleep and lowers inflammation
claims.believers: Advocates say contact with the earth supplies electrons that reduce inflammation and calm the body, and they cite testimonials and small studies.[2][3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that skeptics criticise earthing studies; published trials are small, such as a 16-participant study in massage therapists. [8][4]

claims.claim: Going barefoot feels better than shoes
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says shoes and socks feel tight and constricting compared with grass and stone underfoot.[5]
claims.experts: No published study cited here addresses this preference.

claims.claim: Grounding improves recovery and gives a fresher look through better sleep
claims.believers: Advocates link lower inflammation and calmer stress to better sleep and recovery, which appearance-minded users connect to a rested face and better training. [2][3]
claims.experts: Healthline reports small studies on stress, pain and wound healing but notes that sample sizes are small and placebo was not controlled; none measured appearance. [7]
